In the past almost 30 years we've owned 2 Corollas, a Camry and I'm on my third Taco TRDOR for running around in the dirt.  Also a couple Mazda CX5s, great cars except for the infotainment.

Just yesterday we bought a Kia Sportage PHEV. In terms of comfort, ride quality, quietness, and the integration of the gadgetry it is hands down superior to the RAV4 (yes, local Toy dealer had a couple so we started there), priced similarly. She loves it, all that matters.  We did look at a Prius PHEV, but at our age getting into and out without requiring back surgery afterward made it a no go.

comments.name: theron imbrie
comments.body: GM blew it by killing the Pontiac brand.

comments.name: David Gregory
comments.body:
Toyota also owns interests in Subaru (20%) and Mazda (5%). Both are sharing development work with Toyota. 

Subaru and Toyota are sharing the EV development which has resulted in the current EVs and the soon to come Toyota Highlander and Subaru Getaway 3 row SUVs.

Mazda shares a production plant in Alabama and is using some Toyota ICE platforms.

comments.name: Bruce Fernandes
comments.body:
The big 3 automakers wrote off $60B because Biden gamed the system forcing the big 3 to begin a transition to EVs years too soon for the market.

The market was already showing consumers leaning into hybrids because they were unwilling to be held hostage to being a pure EV when there were big questions about the availability of charging stations.

Hybrids are the perfect transition car to own.  I have many friends regretting the purchase of an EV the first time they traveled and the charging station they were counting on to charge was closed.

comments.name: Steve Gokorsch
comments.body:
When GM decided to share platforms across brands and  kill off Oldsmobile and Pontiac customers were not fooled.  We knew that these were little more than a Chevy with plastic "chrome" trim.  Today there is little difference between a Caddy Escalade and a Chevy Tahoe.  The differentiation is the price...

Meanwhile Toyota kept their corporate identity on all their vehicles and developed very differentiated brands: Corolla, Camry, RAV 4...  Each brand stayed true to the target market needs. 

Too bad.  I really liked my  Oldsmobile with FWD and a 305 V8.  The Pontiac GTO started a new era.

comments.name: David O
comments.body:
“Toyota appeals more to eco-conscious car buyers and those who prioritize reliability and efficiency. GM wins among truck buyers seeking roominess and brawn, and American-brand loyalists.”

Malarkey.  The “eco-conscious buyers” are a small, illogical segment of the market. 

Thanks to Trump’s tariffs Toyota is investing a billion dollars into manufacturing their vehicles here in the US.  The author seems to be trying to put a bad spin on that.

I’ve owned GM’s and Fords and Jeeps and still do.  But my newest is a Lexus plug in hybrid and my choice was based on many factors.  My next vehicle will probably be a Tesla for the self driving abilities.  Consumers make choices based on their personal needs and wants.

But I think it’s great Toyota will be hiring Americans to make vehicles HERE.

comments.name: Randall Pacheco
comments.body: Americans have had to resign ourselves to the fact that Japan makes the best cars and Europe makes the most interesting cars. Recently the WSJ columnist said the best large SUV is made in Korea. MAGA!

articles.title: The Supreme Court’s Popular Mandate
articles.summary: Hakeem Jeffries calls it a MAGA ‘subsidiary.’ A new poll says otherwise.

comments.name: James G.
comments.body: The problems with the Supreme Court cannot be diagnosed by a few rulings that are pro Trump or anti Trump. Instead, the focus should be on the issues hampering the effectiveness of the Court in serving the needs of the country. I see the following concerns: The Court needs an enforceable ethics code. The Court needs modifications so that it can be more productive, i.e., handle more cases, and at a faster pace. Whether this requires additional Justices is open to debate, but what is not open to debate is that the population of the country has increased almost 10-fold since the Court's size was fixed at 9 Justices.The Court should operate year-round.

comments.name: Melanie is here
comments.body:
"The Marquette survey included 1,076 adults nationwide, whose views of the Court are polarized as expected,..."

See, the Court used to enjoy tremendous support of voters because they were seen as trustworthy, stable and above politics. As it should be.  But when they keep voting along party lines, it does feel political.

And the reason that they have voted against some of Trump's cases says more about how outlandishly these were to begin with.  No modern president has requested to play fast and lose with the constitution, or has had to defend paying restitution to a victim of sexual assault at his hands, or has set arbitrary and vindictive tariffs that affect our economy.

comments.name: Joe D
comments.body: It doesn't help matters when our top leaders (Biden, Trump, Harris, Schumer, etc.) denigrate the justices and publicly describe the SCOTUS as a "rogue court" and an "illegitimate court" guilty of a "miscarriage of justice" every time it make a decision that is unpopular with their party.

comments.name: TONY LINVILLE
comments.body: Doing stuff like Jefferies wants to do is how 3rd world countries are born.

comments.name: S Lazzeri
comments.body: Over 1,000 of us were surveyed and one third did not know who John Roberts is?  That is shameful.

comments.name: David Gregory
comments.body:
The Supreme Court has always been political and has often been on the wrong side of history and willing to play along with imaginary things like corporate personhood and birthright citizenship. Or that independent agencies set up by Congress and doing executive functions do not violate the separation of powers.  Or that the Federal Reserve has a right to do what it does.

Al Gore won the Y2K election and a Republican Majority decided to overrule the ruling of the Florida State Supreme Court despite the fact that the states have the right to determine how electors are chosen.

One of the lawyers working on the case for the RNC and Bush - John Roberts.

comments.name: Chip Yonis
comments.body: History will remember Mr Jeffries as one (along with Schumer) who presided over the surrender of the Democrat Party to the Marxists

comments.name: John Brack
comments.body: FDR’s court-packing scheme failed in the 1930s, but the Court soon tacked left for decades. For the left, anything short of total, 99-to-100% judicial compliance with their ideology is treated as a "threat to democracy."

comments.name: Terry Roberts
comments.body:
Hui, they say, “seriously disrupted the socialist market economic order,”.  So he committed crimes against the society. Gee, do you think there are any Americans committing crimes against our society? 

We have a housing crisis super-charged by companies that buy houses to raise and collect rents while struggling young families can't find a home they can afford.

The "Great Communicator", Ronald Reagan drew on historical American antigovernmentalism to create a revolution of anti-tax crapitalism.  So now we have a weak government that bows down to the wealthy who made their money by hook or by crook.  Benefit to society need no longer be considered.

But wait!  Nobody but governments can make (print) new money.  The wealthy don't "make" money, but rather "take" money, without creating any new value to the society.  This is a travesty of what corporations were created for.

  So there is little wonder why Democratic Socialism is gaining steam in America, even as the Party of the Rich screams about the threat of the "radical" Left.  Intelligent Americans are coming to see that the only radicals are on the Right.  Four decades of antigovernmental trickle-down, voodoo Reaganomics is about enough.

comments.name: wolf
comments.body:
That is justice served and accountability recognized in a functioning society.

Laws should always be applied equally to all citizens and examples set for the wealthy privileged and especially government officials.

Here in the U.S. the billionaires and leaders in government have no need for any accountability.  Let's not forget the seditionists on Jan 6 given pardons for being on the "right side" in the attempt to overthrow the results of the election! Let's not forget the ongoing grift and corruption daily.  What a sad and hot mess this country has become.

 So here we have an example of what justice should look like... accountability of actions no matter the wealth and hubris it belongs to.

Way to go with this case of greed and corruption  China.  A good example set.

comments.name: Josh
comments.body:
Hui or Xu, the founder of Evergrande and once the richest in China, was sentenced to life imprisonment, and his two sons, educated in Canada while young, would also go to prison. Much of his wealth was ill-gotten. The company's debts to banks, contractors, and investors totaled more than 2.4 trillion rmb. To put it in perspective, this amount averages about 1,700 rmb for each and every Chinese. This crook was famous for saying that he built housing for sale, and that there would be no need to build after people made advance payments.

One punishment he got is that he would be stripped of political rights for his entire life. Such a punishment is laughable, since it means nothing in China. However, it may be useful to introduce it to America, because a crook and an evil will never have another chance to enjoy political freedoms and rights, let alone getting elected.

comments.name: Raymond Cui
comments.body: Hundreds of high level officials in China would be living a nervous life fron now on because Xu didn't get a death sentence. The only person  who wanted and allowed him to live is Xi Jinping, becasue he knew Xu RMB2.4 trillion (US$260 billion) "debt" didn't just disappear. Other than the RMB80B (US$12B) Xu had transferred to family trusts out of China and a few billions taken by Xi's family (brother and sister), most of the remaining trllion were shared by hundreds of Centnrnal Committee members, state regulatory officials, ministers, provincial and municipal party secretaries and baning and securities officials. The non-death sentencing is a Sword of Damocles, ready to fall any time and over any head Gen Sec Xi decides.

comments.name: Dmitri
comments.body: Not a whole lot different from our own billionaire bankers and developers.

comments.name: DJ
comments.body: Talk about not being able to read the handwriting on the wall. With all his money you would think he would have be living in London, Paris or New York. Well outside the grasp of Chinese law enforcement.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body: Retired Organic Chemistry Professor Here:  we should hire Chinese Prosecutors to go after our dear leader and all his corrupt colleagues, including his book  “The Art of the Deal.”

comments.name: Tom Canty
comments.body: Anyone, smarter than me, see a parallel between Evergrande and our current US, AI version of the Oklahoma land grab?

articles.title: China Sentences Evergrande Founder to Life in Prison
articles.summary: Hui Ka Yan’s punishment caps the downfall of a property empire whose collapse set off a prolonged crisis in the Chinese economy.

comments.name: Melinda Ennis-Roughton
comments.body:
This is so important. My Dad and I were very close.  I was a Daddy’s girl all my life and my well read dad taught me my love of reading, and my values about race and equality. That said, after his 30s, he voted  GOP and we often argued politics. But with Trump it became ugly and for me —inexplicable. My dad hated so much about corporate America—but then he embraced this corrupt corporate creature. In his old age Dad watched Fox 24/7 and became bitter and the proverbial angry old white guy. The last years we had terrible fights and I simply could not accept that my dear father supported the vile creature that is Trump—who for me symbolized everything my father had taught me to reject. After a lifetime of love between us —there was a division at the end that pains me terribly today since I lost him
three years ago.  There are so many reasons to detest what Trump has done to this country. But dividing families like this may be the worst.

comments.name: Gen Zed Cdn. Family
comments.body: So, when and if America's Social Security either runs out of money or greatly reduces its payments to seniors in a few years, will these parents have need to ask their children for a loan?

comments.name: Brian
comments.body: As much as dealing with my conservative relatives can be frustrating, I try to remember that national political issues should not be allowed to destroy my most immediate relationships. That would be a cruel and ultimately pointless inversion.

comments.name: Anonymous
comments.body:
Sounds exhausting, for both the participants and the viewers.

Earlier this year I was trapped in a hotel-bound Uber for over an hour during a snowstorm with a driver who insisted on inflicting her incoherent, baseless MAGA political opinions on me once she learned I was from Oregon, despite my repeated and increasingly unsubtle attempts to change the topic.

Finally, I just relented. I listened to every single point she made, repeated back to her my understanding of her position, and then meticulously dismantled every argument she had put forth. Of course it was pointless; she was completely uninformed and had no ability to think critically, but her vague impressions about reality were more important than any facts. When cornered, she just reverted to debunked talking points from earlier in the conversation.

In the end, she just wanted to have her opinions reinforced, lacked empathy, and had a captive audience to fulfill her emotional need. Her family sounded much like the one described here, so I can empathize with her kids.

comments.name: Grant
comments.body: Democracy is hard. But we all love it as long as other people agree with us.

comments.name: citybumpkin
comments.body:
In supposedly less divisive times, "no politics, no religion" was apparently considered appropriate in social settings. Why do we live in a time when so many people of all political persuasions cannot stop themselves from talking about politics in social settings as if it's some kind of verbal diarrhea? Believe it or not, democracy does not operate on everybody agreeing. There's a reason elections are based on plurality and majority, not unanimity. It seems politics have left the sphere of civics and entered the realm of obsession.

Is this a product of adults overstimulating themselves with political discourse on social media and traditional? It seems many adults need to restrain their own social media access and screen time before they worry about the kids.

comments.name: Jonathan
comments.body: One key element appears to be missing from this YouTube content (or at least the reporting on it): the human impact of “politics.”  “Politics” is not something that can or should be compartmentalized and put away neatly as if it were a board game. The actions and decisions of government officials have an immediate impact on real human beings in tangible (and often devastating) ways. Impact like taking away a person’s liberty and basic human dignity (e.g., plucking them from airports and shoving them in detention centers without any due process, when—before the stroke of Trump’s pen—they had been in the US legally).  While I appreciate that these children are doing the hard work of attempting to educate their parents, I think that the reporting is a bit irresponsible because it ostensibly legitimizes the parents’ position.  And because I am sure MAGA people will claim that I side with the children because I’m a “liberal,” I want to clarify that I say these things simply because I am an educated, analytical person who reads and interprets facts objectively.  Having the ability to discern truth from falsehood is not a political persuasion. Trump’s followers (of which these parents are 2) inexplicably accept as true his unending, provably false claims.

comments.name: DC
comments.body: I will never understand the people who cling to Trump as though he is the Messiah.  We have an elderly aunt who traveled the world working for an airline and regularly visited Mexico for shopping and medical services.  Now she is very pro-Trump and is “afraid” of the migrants coming across the border into AZ where she lives.  When we point out the disparity she doesn’t see the contradiction.  My only explanation is her constant indoctrination by Fox News, which blares from every television in her retirement facility.  Fox News has done more to harm civil discourse and honest discussion than any other entity.

articles.title: The Parents Are MAGA. The Kids Are Liberal. Can YouTube Help?
articles.summary: “The Necessary Conversation,” a podcast and YouTube show, is a very public example of the political disputes families are having all across the country.

articles.title: Darline Graham’s Taiwan Mistake
articles.summary: The South Carolina Senate candidate’s goof wasn’t good, but neither was the answer by her competitor, Ralph Norman.

comments.name: ADAM NEILL
comments.body: So people will elect (call it hire) a person with no experience or knowledge of the job they are to be doing.   Never would have made it through a HR screening.   We are running towards a Idiocracy.

comments.name: Eric Morgan
comments.body: I don't believe the US will be a front-line defender of Taiwan. The (very) best we will see is the US providing weapons for Taiwan to defend itself--with a minimal goal of making the cost of an invasion by China very painful and a maximum goal of preventing any conflict altogether. I just don't see us intervening in a direct conflict with China; we are never going to state that, for obvious reasons.

comments.name: S Lazzeri
comments.body:
Why Ms. Graham believes she is remotely qualified to be a Senator is the same hubris that drives others to run for high office without any prior experience running for even a school board seat.   

We voters need to smarten up.  This is a hiring decision.  Would you hire an accountant for your company with no experience at all?  Or a lawn care company?  Of course not.

comments.name: Bruce Mc
comments.body: And what must the people of Taiwan be thinking as the US has pulled an aircraft carrier from the Pacific to the Persian Gulf, and it's being reported in the news that the US has basically used up all its munitions in Iran?

comments.name: Grant McDonald
comments.body: Most Americans are not foreign policy experts. They barely know where many of these countries are, much less how they fit into the global economic system as in the case of Taiwan. Despite that, politicians at the federal level must understand the complexities of foreign policy. Graham's deflection by saying her constituents "care more about making ends meet", is really her acknowledging she has no idea what she's talking about and not ready for higher office.

comments.name: Bryan Dorsey
comments.body: MAGA DEI hire on full display.

comments.name: John Clarke
comments.body: Her opponent is better qualified, I wonder of South Carolinians care?

comments.name: roger levy
comments.body: When Joe Biden blurted out that the US would go to war to defend Taiwan in the event of an attack, our foreign policy Whiz Kids fell over themselves to publicly correct such an unenlightened, impolitic remark. Not exactly, they assured, with characteristic clarity and conviction. These very same Whiz Kids, after all, had long ago declaimed that the enlightened course for relations with China was to accept that there is only one of them--"One China" uber alles, one might say.  Now the EB--the official scribe of globalist doctrine--suddenly feels compelled to reprimand a candidate's perfectly reasonable reply that she isn't well enough informed on the topic to be goaded into saying something stupid.  Or as incoherent on the subject of Taiwan (e.g. Free China) as some others we know.

comments.name: Spencer
comments.body: If you are traveling in the midwest, do not pass up Bellefontaine and Calvary cemeteries in St. Louis. They stand next to each other and contain a great deal of local American history.

comments.name: Mary Sweeney
comments.body: In the 19th century the Rural Cemetery Movement resulted in the construction of cemeteries that doubled as public parkland. Many of these cemeteries are still in existence and still beautiful. My husband and I have visited several of them and they are generally lovely, peaceful places where, yes, you do confront human mortality but you can also enjoy a nice walk in an attractive green space. My mother (born in 1932) and her sisters sometimes walked to one such cemetery and actually had picnics there when they were young! Recognizing that death is a natural part of life is healthy and having peaceful green spaces to enjoy may actually buy you a few more years of life. Besides, reserving these beautiful spaces only for the dead in a nation where green space is often in short supply makes no sense.

comments.name: AngRN
comments.body: I enjoyed your artical. I am a nurse,  and was 25 when I zipped the body bag  closed of a patient who could have been me- my age, same faith, similiar interests. I wrote my advanced directive soon after,  and became a huge advocate about having the discussion with family about wishes for dying and death. The discussion is the most important part, but to have it written down is a gift to loved ones left behind. I was a hospice nurse for many years, and saw death just as much of a beautiful miracle as birth. I also love cemeteries! My favorites are the Minneapolis Pioneer and Solders Memorial cemetery and Irish Hollow cemetary in Rockland Township,  MI. Lakewood is beautiful too!

comments.name: Julie A
comments.body: Now that my parents are gone, I have become the family grave tender.  There are live flowers on their graves which I visit to take care of, and I put out small artificial bouquets on the others, as they always did - for both sets of my grandparents, some great-grandparents, a great aunt. A few years ago I learned my aunt's 5-year-old little sister had been buried alone; I visit her now too.  I realized she's buried not far from my mom's dear friend who we always referred to as "aunt". In my travels, I discovered many others that I have known who are now laid to rest, and I visit them too to pay my respects. I realized recently that when I am buried in the family plot I will be toe-to-toe with my beloved junior high English teacher, who is still with us but whose grave in her family plot has been pre-engraved with her name.  Not far away are some of the founders of our town who died in the late 1800s.  How my average family wound up among them is a mystery.  I'm glad I went with my parents every year to set out flowers when I was young; after many years away, I feel like I'm getting to know my family and my town all over again in a quiet new way.

comments.name: Tom Wanamaker
comments.body:
I find it comforting to know that nobody has ever cheated death and that it will happen to me too.  (In fact, I would consider immortality a living nightmare that renders one's life meaningless.)  

There's still a lot I want to see and do before I die, but I don't dread my own mortality.

My late father-in-law said in his last year, "I'm ready to die, but if I knew when and where it was going to happen, I wouldn't go there."

comments.name: helene
comments.location: San Miguel De Allende, Gto., Mexico
comments.body: I live in Mexico and almost never pass up a pantheon/cemetery when I see one from my car.  Mexican cemeteries can be humble, beautiful, touching and tranquil except during Dia de Los Muertos when they turn into a riot of marigolds, cockscomb, food, incense, music and love.

comments.name: Mike b
comments.body: a place where I would not want to spend a lot of time - a cemetery.  City parks would be preferable, or a hike in a large park…..but with all those pesky fellow citizens around might ruin the author’s mood.  In a cemetery I would feel like I was intruding on this space, like walking through ICU’s just so I can feel better about not being sick.

comments.name: Arlo A. Brown
comments.body: Urban parks began in the US in the 19th late century because urban planners noticed that people gathered in cemeteries on Sundays to relax in nature.

articles.title: I Spent My Summer in the Cemetery. There, I Found Strange Solace.
articles.summary: In an increasingly morbid world, we can learn from graveyards.

comments.name: Time
comments.body: mind blowingly engaging article about topics normally would find completely uninteresting. Of course, there's more to talk about as to the underlying reasons people in American society continue to try to adapt to a sick culture rather than become sane, but that's off-topic. Nice.

comments.name: Cela
comments.body: I challenge the whole premise of this article - that the problem with the Democrats is that they are poor actors who are using the wrong techniques and approaches.  All that feckless nullities like Schumer and Jeffries believe in is cashing payments from corporate lobbyists and the Israel lobby.  If they were compelled to speak on that, they would have a power and persuasion that would put Brando to shame.  But, asked to speak on the problems of our nation, and they are empty and silent.  What we need are people with a naturally emerging passion who know what it is like to suffer in this unbelievably wealthy and unbelievably unequal society.

comments.name: Thomas
comments.body:
The author is somewhat on the nose about acting and politics. The best movies, and actors, can cogently and clearly tell a story.  Lack of clarity in messaging, and unnecessary complexity, is the downfall of Democrats. 

Everything in the 2026 midterms should be linked to 3 symptoms of the situation we are in: what I call the I.C.U. situation.
I for Inflation
C for Corruption
U For Unconstitutional. 

Every question must be clearly and immediately linked to these three symptoms. Whether on housing, Israel-Palestine, immigration, trans rights or election security, all answers can be linked to one or more of these symptoms.

comments.name: Lawyermom
comments.body:
I studied with Sanford Meisner so I know of what you write.
As a voter, it drives me up the wall that so much of our politics is due to a candidate’s “performance” in a debate, press conference, or whatever.  I wish US voters would spend more time researching the candidates from neutral sources rather than evaluating stage presence.  I have cast community theater and I have cast ballots.  In my mind, the 2 have nothing in common.
If a candidate is plausible, has a good resume, and supports the same issues as I do, that’s who is getting my vote.  Reagan, Clinton, Obama and Trump have all been gifted performers but they are leagues apart as presidents.  
Finally, this performance-based judgement is extremely unfair to women.  Both HRC and Kamala Harris had the experience to make them good presidents.  Unfortunately, a lot of men couldn’t get past their obviously female gender.

comments.name: Feisty New Yorker
comments.body: This article was spot on.  I had read about Hakeem Jeffries' positions in this newspaper and on the internet, agreed, and wanted to see him "live."  So I watched a Sunday show.  Midway through his interview, I realized Jeffries was spouting out pre-prepared talking points.  There was no fire in the belly, no passion, no desire to correct wrongs. He could have been a robot.  I am still voting D because the alternative is disaster.  But I would like someone to actually vote for.

comments.name: Steve Paradis
comments.body:
Consultancy
If you don't have a solution, you can still make money on the problem.

(Now let's hear from the consultants who promoted Graham Platner. He was soooo believable.)

comments.name: Number 25
comments.body: Sure Dems have communications issues, but nobody embodies inauthenticity quite as well as JD Vance.

comments.name: Andrew
comments.body: My interpretation of  Connor Lounsbury's article is that in order to win an election, it's more important to focus on performance just like what an actor/actress would, and forget about authenticity.  Ronald Reagan might be an excellent example of a successful politician who started out as an actor.  He's got a point!  But I would favor authenticity over performance in a politician.  That's why D. J. Trump is a successful politician.  He comes across as crude but very believable.  Of course, he may be putting on nothing more than a phony act just an actor/actress could, so to me, look at the issues.  Where do the politicians stand?  Do you agree with them?  Do you disagree with them?  Are their reasons logical?  Are their reasons emotional?  Whether their reasons are logical or emotional, more than anything, do they make sense?  Are they consistent?  Are they truthful?  Are they misleading?  I'm done writing now.

articles.title: Great Actors Are More Believable Than Democrats
articles.summary: Democrats often don’t sound as if they believe themselves. To fix that, they should listen more to acting teachers and less to pollsters.

comments.name: M. L.
comments.body: I use Uber because it is what I've always used and I'm afraid to try new things.  That said, I notice that most drivers here have both an Uber and a Lyft sticker and they're running both apps.  Between two apps/companies, if the price is similar and the drivers are the same, is there really a difference?

comments.name: Jane
comments.body: I have never understood why anyone wants to attract flies.....with either honey or vinegar....

comments.name: Notorious SJV
comments.body: I used to always use Lyft when I could, because Travis Kalanick was such a jerk, but today I am less loyal. I use Uber sometimes because my Amex card includes a monthly Uber credit, and that's free money. I check prices for both before I commit, and I check arrival times. The problem with the latter is that quoted arrival times are almost always a lie.

comments.name: John Conroy
comments.body:
My wife and I have now ridden in a Waymo autonomous cab three times in West Los Angeles traffic with no problems. I make a point of closely observing how Waymo cars drive when I'm walking and driving around L.A. So far, I'm impressed. A recent news story in USA Today noted that women in particular prefer taking Waymo because they don't have to worry about male drivers' behavior. Turns out that Lucia, a good friend of my wife and me, has been using Waymo for a while now, partly for that reason.

Waymo cars don't flip me off, cut me off, or shoot at me. Now we can add Lyft drivers making false vomit claims to the list of Waymo benefits, I guess.

comments.name: Marion Julia Fenton Ford
comments.body:
I had been using Uber as the Lyft cars were very low to ground and I’m disabled. Uner seemed to offer more choice. For quite a price. But when I was too ill to safely drive myself… 
Relative came down to help me during the surgery and we both took the Uber. She is very chatty and was speaking of the exchange students. Her aunt used to host and how wonderful their English was. She did not realise that this could cause an international incident. She lives in a wealthy area in NY. 
Shortly thereafter I received a warn off letter from Uber telling me to stop bringing my unscheduled five children and many other things. I order an SUV level Vehicle in order to accommodate my wheelchair easily and pay through the nose for it. No children anywhere ever. I am on the sidewalk waiting for the vehicle. Occasionally, I have seen the car slow and then accelerate past me not wanting to deal with a disabled person I gather. I then have to start from Scratch and put in a request for the Uber from the sidewalk again. 
Thankfully, my surgeries are over. My car and I have been serviced and are ready for the road. So thankfully, I am no longer in need of Uber. It was an extremely expensive and frustrating time of my life.
Not edited for talk to text transcription errors. Life is just too short.

comments.name: Kent
comments.body: I had a nearly identical experience with Lyft, photos and all.  It seemed to be the same car in my case, but the fact was that it wasn’t me who got sick in it.  It took the same amount of effort to break through the wall of prompts and automated responses to get to an apparent human, but ultimately Lyft credited back the damage fee based on the fact that I had never been accused of damaging a car previously. So I guess some Lyft riders make a habit of such things? Feels like a scam on the part of certain drivers.

comments.name: Alex
comments.body: If a NYT reader is going to Portugal or Spain, watch out for this Uber scam. Three times out of six rides, They scammed us by telling us during the ride that we entered the wrong destination location and threatened to drop us off, at some random location, unless we cancelled the ride and rebook it. By the last Uber ride to the departing Lisbon airport, I had caught on to the scam and flat out refused to "cancel" the ride while the driver continually threatened to drop us off at a "Goto Cafe" which he claimed I had incorrectly entered into the app. After 15 minutes of harassment, we were at the airport terminal. We get out and enter the terminal where we saw promptly saw a cafe named "Go to Coffee"!

comments.name: Evan
comments.body:

It is unfortunate that this article does not mention the full range of options for treatment resistant depression. 

Although TMS, ketamine/esketamine, and psychedelics (e.g. psilocybin) have received much recent publicity, ECT remains the gold standard of care for severe treatment resistant depression or catatonia. Many patients benefit from a tricyclic antidepressant (e.g., nortriptyline or imipramine)  or a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) (e.g., phenelzine, tranylcypromine) but have never been offered one of these. Every individual with treatment resistant depression should also receive treatment with an evidence based treatment such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Psychotherapy is not just chatting about day-to-day aspects of one's week but should  be a structured and evidence based approach to gaining insight into (and modifying) one's thought processes and behavior. These can be especially engrained with treatment resistant depression and can take years of concerted effort to establish new patterns of coping/interaction.  

Two messages deserve emphasis: 
1. For individuals with treatment resistant depression, there are many more options than discussed in this article! Don't lose hope!!!
2. For anyone involved in health policy and payment (such as insurers), please authorize appropriate treatments for treatment resistant depression. Although months/years of psychotherapy or meds/ECT/TMS may be required, the benefits for patients and society can be huge!

The other reason is that the tariffs are a national sales tax, similar to the value-added taxes that Canada and Europe have. A national sales that called itself that would be politically untenable and couldn’t get through Congress. But a back-door sales tax in the form of tariffs gets over political hurdles.

With a $40 trillion debt, the U.S. is desperate for any revenue it can find, and our tariff-based national sales tax is bringing in money. “The U.S. government collected roughly $195 billion in customs duties and tariffs during fiscal year 2025, a sharp increase over prior years.” (AI overview.) I enjoy reading articles about public cameras and the surveillance state, their radical detractors and their law-man defenders--mostly to laugh at the hyperbole and shrill doomsaying.

This article delivers a surprise ending--Willy Staley makes the observation that the paranoia of the anti-camera crowd is comically misplaced. I agree. 

Fears about a future police-surveillance state are taking place in a present police-surveillance state. 

The right to cast one's eyes, in public, wherever one chooses to, is implied in the constitution, protected by statute, and widely appreciated. When cameras became a reality, the same protections were extended--if it is in public, and your eyes can see it, it is legal to record it with a device. What's more, your ownership of that image is protected by law. 

Those rights, enjoyed by individuals, extend to institutions such as the media and law enforcement. (What you, or the police, DO with those images is regulated by laws aimed at harm reduction.) 

Therefore, opposition to Flock cameras themselves, as opposed to the uses of the images produced, is opposition to the individual's right to "record what their eyes can see." 

Let's not throw the baby out with the bath water.

At New College of Oxford, founded some time in the 1380s, there was a clump of oak trees that was carefully kept for centuries, the need to upkeep them passing down through the grounds keepers. At one point in the 20th century, the administration discovered the reason: the oak beams in the celling of the chapel had become "beetley," and they had to be replaced. The oak clump had been maintained for just such eventuality, for every Englishman would know that oak beams eventually go "beetly" and have to be replaced. I taught at New College of Hofstra, which was modeled on its Oxford counterpart, with which it maintained a loose relationship. I learned this story from the Dean of the College, Mr. David Christman.

Later, the American discovers that the correct fare is actually 20 Gryvna (the local currency which is worth less).

So when, a week later, the American happens to hail a cab driven by the same cabbie, he is irate. "Hey," he says. "You charged me $20 when the real fare is 20 Gryvna. What gives?"

The cabbie looks mournfully over his shoulder and says: "Look. I knew the real fare is 20 Gryva. But $20 is very beautiful."

You can't defeat a people who have this kind of humor. This splendid, brave, and charming people.

Long live Ukraine!  Slava Ukraini!

Even before the SDSers took over academia in late '60s and '70s, most academics, who had never had any contact with business or the private sector, considered any such contact almost a Mark of Cain. We, the newly elect students admitted to nirvana, were not so subtly steered to "respectable" academia and government, to "save humanity" (see Keynesian economics) or some such mission, and to look down upon those who were merely money-grubbing capitalists. Some of us, especially those who came from less exalted and wealthy families, began to notice, however, that the Leftism and Statism they preached rested on a base of ... previous money-grubbing capitalists....who, on closer examination, mostly got their fortunes by actually serving and innovating for real people as opposed to pontificating in ivory towers. The devil is in the details and when you look deeply at projects like these you find 80-90% are market rate or very close to market rate apartments, which, to most New Yorkers, are not affordable. Usually only 5-10% of apartments offered are anywhere close to what people think are truly affordable. For example, the $2,200 cited in this piece as the lowest price for some (# is not stated) apartments in the towers being planned, are most likely for studios. To many working class New Yorkers this is not affordable.  To the supply siders who have owned the narrative that says we have to build more and more units to achieve housing affordability, the econ 101 argument that more supply will invariably lead to lower prices, the NYC housing market is not a perfect market and is governed by speculative players, so the law of supply and demand does not behave as you think it will. We can't build our way to affordability.

I work in the holistic health sector, and I’ve long had some serious reservations about Bryan Johnson.

When it comes to his protocols, we are learning a great deal about how the body works, but there is still far more we don’t know.

How the body’s finely regulated systems are affected by a very large number of supplements—at one point he claimed to be taking upwards of 100 pills a day—is hard to say.

I’m not suggesting that his autoimmune gastritis resulted from this, but supplementation beyond the treatment of gross deficiency is still a relatively young field.

We don't know whether extreme supplementation regimens could disrupt normal physiological balance or create nutrient imbalances.

What we do know is that chronic stress can meaningfully affect immune function, and in people who are already predisposed to autoimmune disease it may sometimes trigger the onset of symptoms.

And while I can't speak for Mr. Johnson personally, I would find his intense and highly regimented health routine incredibly stressful.

When it comes to longevity, maintaining one's health through a healthy diet, exercise, adequate sleep, and stress management is certainly worthwhile, even though none of these can guarantee an exceptionally long life.

Longevity or not, good health certainly allows for a far better quality of life.

But if the goal becomes keeping the body functioning for as many years as possible, almost to the exclusion of everything else, it certainly begs the question: why?

Bryan constantly says that 90 percent of the benefit can be add for essentially no money - getting 8 hours of sleep, eating healthy, and exercising. One of the most effective interventions he did was 20 minutes of sauna a day.

His exercise program is build around Ben Patrick's Knees Over Toes, which is available free on Youtube and requires almost no equipment.

Everyone says "he look terrible" but I've met him in person. He not only looks healthy, he walks and moves like someone in his 20's. 

People love to hate on Bryan, but there are a lot more people out there more worth of opprobrium than Bryan.

Physicians have historically treated aging as an inevitability, but why not treat it as any other condition that we can delay and manage? We will likely never get to immortality, but if we change our paradigm and challenge ourselves to be more thoughtful about how our actions and interventions interact with our biology, we can likely get a few more healthy years than previous generations. I for one would love a few more good years with my family and friends.

I am a 72 year-old former NIH Scientist trying to make sense of Zeke Emanuel's arbitrary formula; it's a strangely familiar echo of the "I never want to live past 30" meme which I heard with some frequency in NYC in the 70s. I think aiming for 150 years is narcissistic crazy, but 75 is too self-limiting.  I know and have known many 75+ scientists who are still contributing.  Ernst Mayr, a distinguished biologist who lived to be 100 often argued that because his field, systematics, dealt with the immense, historic complexity of nature, master taxonomists only reach their peak after decades of continuous exposure to organisms.  I attended 86 year-old Victor McKusick's funeral in 2008; Victor is often referred to as the father of medical genetics, my specialty.  

Of course aging can be painful, with the most frail elderly living a life consisting mainly of medical appointments.  But, there are solutions to that which don't require transfusions and transplants from sources of long telomeres, like Bryan Johnson.  The verses of Ecclesiastes that Pete Seeger put to music seem wise at my age.

If our combined household income is 400k, that would qualify us as wealthy by most peoples standards.  I still can't afford to pay 80k a year after taxes for school.  That would entail devoting half of my pre-tax earnings to her tuition.

The reality is that even so called wealthier families have trouble paying the crazy tuitions, and have to factor in total cost.

Why has college gotten so expensive?  I'd look at how the gov't handles loans to students, and the industry designed to keep them paying interest for their entire working lives.  It's very profitable for large banks, and risk free.  When the money is easy to get, the tuition keeps going higher.

To be clear, I believe in higher education and believe that finances should not be a barrier but this needs to be based on a broader public policy. Over the last 40-50 years, college tuition list price has increased at twice the rate of inflation, much of that driven by a huge increase in administrative costs. Not far behind are the rising cost of "creature comforts" demanded by current students.

The rapid escalation of the list price has transformed the pricing into a pure negotiated price system.  Why is there such a huge range of price?  Because it is now based on negotiating skill rather than the value provided.  Rather than look at how the list price for college has skyrocketed, how has the average net tuition increased over the decades?  How much cross-subsidizing is there?  Everyone who pays above the average is subsidizing those who pay below the average.

This is about something broader than college financial aid: the ability of the upper classes to hoard advantage while persuading themselves the result is “merit.”

It starts long before college. Wealthy families buy tutors, test prep, coaches, admissions consultants. They know how to work school systems and pursue every accommodation. There’s an uncomfortable class dimension when affluent families have far greater access to ADHD evaluations, leaving one student with a timed exam while another, already backed by years of tutoring and prep, gets substantially more time.

Then there’s the curated extracurrics: the summer trip to Costa Rica to “build houses,” where teenagers are handed a hammer and a nail, do a few hours of supervised service, then come home with an essay about discovering poverty. Affluence repackaged as character.

And now “merit aid”: colleges discounting tuition for families perfectly capable of paying because those students are financially attractive. It’s a pricing strategy. But call it merit and everyone feels better: the college gets the affluent student, the family gets a discount, and the student gets another credential suggesting all those accumulated advantages were somehow earned.

That is the part of this system we talk about far too little:
Privilege is most durable when it no longer looks like privilege. It looks like merit.
